title: The three-small-triangles conjecture for five points
source: Matthew Kahle, “Points in a triangle forcing small triangles”, arXiv:0811.2449 (2008). (https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.2449), Conjecture 3.1
statement:
Call a triangle **small** if its area is at most $1/4$. Given five points in a triangle of unit area, consider the triangles determined by triples of the five points. **Three-small-triangles conjecture.** The five points determine at least three small triangles.

The claim would strengthen the preceding result, which guarantees only one small triangle. The source notes that three cannot be replaced by four for the displayed configuration; if true, the conjecture would imply corresponding lower bounds for larger point sets by averaging.
summary: For any triangle of area 1 in the plane and any five points of the closed triangle (not necessarily distinct), at least three of the ten unordered triples of the points span a triangle of area at most 1/4, where degenerate triples count with area 0. This is Kahle's three-small-triangles conjecture; three cannot be replaced by four. The proof is a case analysis on the midpoint subdivision with a determinant identity; the reduction from an arbitrary triangle to a standard one is proved in Lean.
paste_summary: Proved. Any five points in a closed triangle of unit area determine at least three triangles of area at most 1/4 (unordered triples; degenerate triples count as area 0; the threshold is inclusive). This is Conjecture 3.1 of Kahle, arXiv:0811.2449; the number three is sharp.
caveat: Degenerate triples are counted as small, the convention forced by the source's use of Soifer's one-triangle theorem. Soifer's book chapter on the problem (Springer) was not read; it is understood to reprint the 2008 material. Bounded literature search only.
